title: Early-period width corrections did not show a clear score gain for NOAA hurricane count ranges in 2014-2025
abstract: A prior study assigned most missed NOAA seasonal hurricane outcomes to narrow ranges. We test whether an early fitted width rule transfers to later seasons. We fit one location shift or one symmetric extension per basin, issue month and count type on 99 ranges from 2003-2013. We test 108 count ranges in 2014-2025. Extension raised coverage from 68.5% to 88.0%, but mean central 70% interval score rose from 8.688 to 8.978. The paired score change was +0.290, with a 95% year-bootstrap interval from -0.759 to +1.219. Fixed shifts kept the mean width unchanged and gave a score change of -0.123 (-0.556 to +0.309). Neither rule showed a clear score gain. Extension helped the eastern Pacific and hurt the Atlantic in subgroup means. Rolling fits also gave no clear gain. An independent parser reproduced all 207 count outcomes from HURDAT2. These results limit the transfer of an early width correction; they do not overturn historical undercoverage. The test has only 12 later years, uses an inherited archive and a split informed by prior results, and evaluates central ranges although NOAA states a coverage target without equal tails. Code, fitted parameters, aggregate evidence, exact input hashes and a figure are included. External source records stay outside the bundle.

display.caption: Fixed rules trained on 2003-2013 count ranges were tested on 108 ranges in 2014-2025. Bars show coverage. Points show mean score changes from issued ranges; lower is better. Lines show 95% year-bootstrap intervals. Widening increased coverage but did not give a clear score gain.
